title: Bilingue
intro: Le dernier sommet : grammaire de haut vol, nuances fines, proverbes et prononciation sans faute. Au bout du chemin, tu seras vraiment bilingue.

boss.name: L'Ultime Bilingue
boss.taunt: Tu te crois bilingue ? It's high time you proved it. Je connais tous les pièges des deux langues… et je ne prononce jamais le k de knife.
boss.defeat: Impossible… Tu es vraiment bilingue ! Bon, every cloud has a silver lining : j'ai enfin trouvé un adversaire à ma hauteur.

units.title: Grammaire de haut vol
units.goal: Maîtriser les structures avancées : it's time + passé, would rather, had better, as if, should inversé et le subjonctif anglais.

lesson.text: Tu connais déjà [[If I were you]] : un verbe au **passé** qui ne parle pas du passé, mais d'une situation **imaginaire** ou **souhaitée**. Les anglophones adorent ce truc ! Voici les structures qui font sonner ton anglais comme celui d'un pro.

lesson.title: It's (high) time + passé
lesson.text: Pour dire « il est (grand) temps que… », on met un **sujet + verbe au passé**, même si on parle de maintenant : [[It's time we left.]] [[It's high time you cleaned your room!]] Jamais ~~It's time we go~~. Sans sujet, on garde l'infinitif : [[It's time to leave.]]

lesson.title: would rather et had better
lesson.text: [[would rather]] (aimer mieux) : avec le **même sujet**, verbe à la base : [[I'd rather stay home.]] [[I would rather walk than take the bus.]] Avec un **autre sujet**, verbe au **passé** : [[I'd rather you didn't tell anyone.]] [[had better]] (ferais mieux de, conseil fort ou avertissement) + base verbale, **sans to** : [[You'd better hurry.]] Ici, le 'd veut dire **had**.

head: Structure
Sens
Exemple
rows: [[She talks as if she knew everything.]]
[[If we were to lose, we would be out.]]
[[You can go, provided that you are home by ten.]]
[[Take a sweater in case it gets cold.]]
[[The coach insisted that he be on time.]]
It is essential / important that + base
[[It is essential that she arrive early.]]

lesson.title: Le subjonctif anglais
lesson.text: Oui, l'anglais a un subjonctif ! Après [[insist that]], [[suggest that]], [[recommend that]], [[It is essential that]]… on met le verbe à la **base** pour tout le monde : pas de -s, et [[be]] pour tous les sujets. [[The doctor recommended that he drink more water.]] [[Mom insisted that everyone be ready by seven.]] On entend aussi [[should]] + base : [[that he should drink]].

items.en: It's high time we went home.
items.fr: Il est grand temps qu'on rentre.

items.en: I'd rather you didn't use my phone.

lesson.text: Pièges de francophone : ~~It's time we go~~ → [[It's time we went]]. ~~I'd rather you don't~~ → [[I'd rather you didn't]]. ~~You'd better to go~~ → [[You'd better go]]. ~~in case it will rain~~ → [[in case it rains]] (jamais will après in case, comme après if). Et attention : [[in case]] (au cas où, par précaution) n'est pas [[if]] (si) !

reading.title: The Great Family Meeting
reading.text:
Every year, before the family camping trip to Algonquin Park, Olivia's mother calls what she proudly names the Great Family Meeting. This year was no different.

“It's high time we talked about the rules,” she announced, sitting at the kitchen table with a notebook. Olivia's little brother, Félix, groaned as if he had been asked to climb a mountain.

The first rule was simple. Mom insisted that everyone be ready by seven in the morning on Saturday. “Should anyone oversleep,” she added, “they will carry the heaviest backpack.” Félix suddenly looked very awake.

The second rule was about screens. “I'd rather you didn't bring your tablets,” Dad said. “We're going camping, not to an arcade.” Olivia wanted to argue, but she knew she had better choose her battles. Instead, she asked if she could bring her camera. Dad agreed, provided that she shared the photos with Grandma.

Then came the food. Félix suggested that they eat only marshmallows for the whole weekend. Everyone laughed except Mom, who wrote down a long list of vegetables. “Bring extra socks too,” she said, “in case it rains. And it always rains.”

Finally, Olivia raised her hand. “I have a rule too. If we were to see a moose, I would be the one who takes the picture.” Félix protested, but the family voted, and Olivia won.

That night, Olivia lay in bed and smiled. She would never admit it, but she secretly loved the Great Family Meeting. For her, it was the moment when summer really began.

questions.q: Why did Félix suddenly look very awake?
choices: He had just drunk a hot chocolate.
He didn't want to carry the heaviest backpack.
He was excited about seeing a moose.
His mother turned on all the lights.

questions.q: Under what condition could Olivia bring her camera?
choices: If she left her tablet at home
If she shared the photos with her grandmother

questions.q: Why does Mom want everyone to bring extra socks?
What does Mom's comment “And it always rains” suggest?
choices: She has never been camping before.
She hopes it will rain this year.
It has rained on many of their past camping trips.

questions.q: What does “she had better choose her battles” mean here?
choices: She decided not to argue about everything.
She wanted to fight with her brother.
She chose to play a video game instead.

questions.q: How does Olivia really feel about the family meeting?
choices: She finds it boring and useless.
She is afraid of her parents' rules.
She wants to cancel it next year.
She enjoys it, even if she doesn't say so.

units.title: Nuances et connotations
units.goal: Choisir le mot juste selon sa connotation : positive, neutre ou négative.

lesson.text: Deux mots peuvent avoir le même sens de base, mais pas la même « couleur ». Dire de quelqu'un qu'il est [[slim]], c'est un compliment. [[thin]], c'est neutre. [[skinny]], c'est souvent négatif (trop maigre). C'est ce qu'on appelle la **connotation**. Un mot mal choisi, et ton compliment devient une insulte !

lesson.title: Des verbes pleins de nuances
lesson.text: **Regarder** : [[glance]] (jeter un coup d'œil rapide), [[peek]] (regarder en cachette), [[stare]] (fixer longtemps), [[glare]] (fusiller du regard, en colère). **Parler** : [[whisper]] (chuchoter), [[mutter]] (marmonner, souvent mécontent), [[yell]] (crier). **Rire** : [[giggle]] (petit rire aigu, nerveux), [[chuckle]] (petit rire discret, dans sa barbe). **Marcher** : [[stroll]] (flâner), [[stride]] (marcher à grands pas, sûr de soi), [[stumble]] (trébucher).

lesson.title: Comment choisir ?
lesson.text: Demande-toi : est-ce que je veux **complimenter**, **décrire** ou **critiquer** ? Pour une grand-mère qui économise intelligemment : [[thrifty]]. Pour quelqu'un qui refuse de partager une seule chip : [[stingy]]. Le contexte décide toujours !

items.en: You look so slim in that jacket!
items.fr: Tu as l'air tellement mince dans ce manteau !

items.en: Stop being so nosy; it's my diary!

lesson.text: Pièges de francophone : [[notorious]] ne veut **pas** dire « notoire » au sens neutre : c'est **célèbre pour quelque chose de mal** ! Et [[cheap]] peut vouloir dire « pas cher »… mais aussi « de mauvaise qualité » ou « radin ». Pour un compliment, dis plutôt [[inexpensive]] ou [[affordable]].

lines.en: Sure. And I'm not stubborn, I'm determined.
lines.fr: Bien sûr. Et moi, je ne suis pas têtue, je suis déterminée.

grammar.q: Tu veux faire un compliment à ta tante sur sa nouvelle silhouette : « You look so ___! »
grammar.explain: slim = mince, c'est un compliment. skinny (maigre) est souvent négatif.

grammar.q: Your friend never gives up and trains every single day. You admire her. She is ___.
grammar.explain: Tu l'admires : il faut le mot positif, determined. stubborn (têtu) est négatif.

grammar.q: The neighbour always reads other people's mail. Which word best describes him?
grammar.explain: Lire le courrier des autres, c'est fouiner : nosy (négatif). curious est neutre ou positif.

grammar.q: Ana wouldn't even share one chip with her best friend. She's so ___!
grammar.explain: Refuser de partager, c'est être radin : stingy. thrifty (économe) est un compliment.

grammar.q: Everyone on our street complains about Rex, the dog who digs up gardens. He is ___ in the neighbourhood.
grammar.explain: Tout le monde se plaint : il est célèbre pour quelque chose de mal → notorious.

grammar.q: Jaden ___ at the answers when the teacher wasn't looking.
grammar.explain: peek = regarder en cachette. Parfait quand le prof ne regarde pas !

grammar.q: The teacher ___ at us when we talked during the test.
grammar.explain: glare = fusiller du regard, en colère. Au passé : glared.

grammar.explain: Une odeur agréable : scent. (stink, c'est une odeur horrible !)

grammar.q: We ___ through the market, looking at everything.
grammar.explain: stroll = flâner, marcher sans se presser. Au passé : strolled.

grammar.q: Stop being so ___; it's just a board game!
grammar.explain: childish = puéril, négatif. childlike (émerveillé) est positif.

grammar.q: He ___ at his watch and ran to the bus.
grammar.explain: glance = regarder très vite. Au passé : glanced.

grammar.q: This bike is ___ but solid: a great deal!
grammar.explain: C'est un compliment : inexpensive (ou affordable). cheap ferait penser à de la mauvaise qualité.

grammar.q: My grandma saves money and never wastes anything; she is so stingy and smart.
grammar.explain: C'est un compliment (smart) : il faut le mot positif thrifty (économe). stingy veut dire radin.

grammar.q: My grandpa looked at the first snow with childish wonder.
grammar.explain: L'émerveillement d'enfant, c'est positif : childlike. childish veut dire puéril.

grammar.q: This garbage bin has a horrible scent.
grammar.explain: scent est une odeur agréable. Pour une poubelle : stink (ou smell).

grammar.q: He glanced at me for ten whole minutes without saying a word.
grammar.explain: glance = un coup d'œil rapide. Pendant dix minutes, on fixe : stared.

reading.title: Same Cat, Different Words
reading.text:
Our English teacher gave us a strange assignment: describe the same moment twice, once as a fan and once as a critic. Zoé chose her neighbour's cat, Biscuit. Here is what she wrote.

Version one: Biscuit is a slim, elegant cat with a curious mind. Every morning, she strolls across our garden as if she owned it. She is determined: when she wants to come inside, she waits patiently at the door until someone opens it. Her owner, an old man with a childlike smile, is thrifty and makes her toys out of old socks. When Biscuit sees me, she glances at me with her bright green eyes, then goes back to her nap in the sun.

Version two: Biscuit is a skinny, nosy cat who sticks her face into everybody's business. Every morning, she wanders through our garden as if she owned it. She is stubborn: when she wants to come inside, she stares at the door and meows until someone gives up. Her owner is so stingy that he makes her toys out of old socks. When Biscuit sees me, she glares at me with her cold green eyes, then goes back to sleeping all day, the lazy thing.

Zoé's teacher wrote one comment at the bottom of the page: “Same cat, same facts, completely different story. Well done.”

Zoé smiled when she read it. She had learned something important: choosing a word is like choosing a pair of glasses. The world stays the same, but it changes what everyone else sees. From now on, she decided, she would choose her glasses very carefully, especially when writing about her little brother.

questions.q: What was the assignment?
choices: To write a story about a lost cat
To describe the same moment twice, from two different points of view
To write a poem about glasses

questions.q: In version two, which word replaces “determined”?
How is the owner described in version two?
What attitude toward Biscuit does version one show?
Why does the teacher write “Same cat, same facts”?
choices: Because Zoé copied the same text twice
Because the facts don't change; only the connotation of the words does
Because both versions are too short

questions.q: What does Zoé's last decision suggest?
choices: She will stop writing about her family.
She knows her word choices could make her brother look good or bad.
She thinks her brother is a cat.

units.title: Phrasal verbs et proverbes
units.goal: Utiliser des phrasal verbs avancés et placer le bon proverbe au bon moment.

lesson.text: Les anglophones parlent avec des **phrasal verbs** (verbe + petit mot) et des **proverbes** à tout bout de champ. Les connaître, c'est comprendre les vraies conversations, les films et les séries… et répondre du tac au tac !

head: Phrasal verb
Sens
Exemple
rows: [[I can't put up with this noise.]]
[[He cheated and got away with it.]]
[[I look up to my big sister.]]
[[I ran into my teacher at the mall.]]
[[The test turned out to be easy.]]
[[She fell out with her best friend.]]
[[The movie didn't live up to the book.]]

lesson.title: Séparable ou pas ?
lesson.text: Les phrasal verbs à **trois mots** ne se séparent jamais : [[put up with it]], [[make up for it]]. Certains verbes à deux mots sont **séparables** ([[figure out]], [[bring up]]) : avec un **pronom**, le pronom va obligatoirement **au milieu** : [[figure it out]], jamais ~~figure out it~~. Après [[end up]] et [[make up for]], le verbe prend **-ing** : [[We ended up eating sushi.]] [[I'll make up for being late.]]

head: Proverbe anglais
Équivalent français
Quand l'utiliser
rows: Les gestes valent mieux que les paroles.
ça arrive en retard, mais ça arrive
À quelque chose malheur est bon.
L'avenir appartient à ceux qui se lèvent tôt.
[[Don't count your chickens before they hatch.]]
Il ne faut pas vendre la peau de l'ours avant de l'avoir tué.
C'est plus facile à dire qu'à faire.
un conseil simple mais difficile à suivre

lesson.text: Pièges de francophone : « supporter » quelqu'un = [[put up with]], pas [[support]] (qui veut dire soutenir, encourager) ! [[look up to]] (admirer) n'est pas [[look up]] (chercher dans le dictionnaire). Et les proverbes ne se traduisent **jamais** mot à mot : on ne dit pas ~~Better late that never~~, ni « sell the bear's skin » : on apprend la version anglaise par cœur.

lines.en: Did you hear? Ethan fell out with Noah over a hockey card.
lines.fr: As-tu entendu ? Ethan s'est brouillé avec Noah à cause d'une carte de hockey.

lines.en: Actions speak louder than words. Let's see if he brings him a real one.
lines.fr: Les gestes valent mieux que les paroles. On verra s'il lui apporte une vraie carte.

reading.title: The Science Fair
reading.text:
Sofia and Samuel had been best friends since kindergarten, so nobody expected them to fall out with each other two weeks before the science fair.

It started with a simple question: whose project was it, really? Sofia said that the idea of building a solar-powered fan had been hers. Samuel said that an idea was useless if nobody could make it work. Neither of them was willing to give up, and soon they weren't even sitting together at lunch.

Their teacher, who had seen this kind of thing before, didn't take sides. She simply reminded them that the project would not finish itself. “You can put up with each other for two more weeks,” she said with a smile, “or you can both start from scratch.”

Neither of them wanted to start again. So, for a few days, they worked in silence. Then something unexpected happened. While looking for a missing screw, Sofia came across Samuel's notebook. On the first page, he had written: “Sofia's idea. Make it work!”

She felt terrible. Samuel had figured out how to make the fan spin, and he had only wanted some credit for that. He had never claimed that the idea was his. He had simply been tired of being ignored.

The next morning, Sofia brought him a hot chocolate to make up for her behaviour. Samuel looked surprised, then laughed. “Better late than never,” he said.

Their fan didn't win first prize. It ended up in third place, behind a robot and a volcano. But when they walked out of the gym together, laughing again like old times, they both knew they had won something more important.

He accepts her apology, even though it came late.

questions.q: What is the “something more important” that they won?
choices: A trip to a science museum

units.title: Le grand oral
units.goal: Déjouer les pièges de prononciation de l'anglais et comprendre un long reportage audio.

lesson.text: Dernière étape ! En anglais, l'orthographe et la prononciation ne s'entendent pas toujours très bien. Des lettres muettes, des mots qui sonnent pareil, des accents toniques qui changent le sens… Les connaître, c'est parler et écrire comme un vrai bilingue.

head: Mot
Lettre muette
Ça sonne à peu près comme

lesson.title: Les homophones : même son, sens différent
lesson.text: [[knight]] (chevalier) / [[night]] (nuit). [[weather]] (météo) / [[whether]] (si). [[peace]] (paix) / [[piece]] (morceau). [[right]] (droite, correct) / [[write]] (écrire). [[hear]] (entendre) / [[here]] (ici). [[flour]] (farine) / [[flower]] (fleur). À l'oral, aucun problème ; à l'écrit, c'est le piège parfait !

lesson.title: L'accent tonique qui change le sens
lesson.text: Pour beaucoup de mots de deux syllabes, le **nom** a l'accent sur la **première** syllabe et le **verbe** sur la **deuxième** : [[a REcord]] (un disque, un record) / [[to reCORD]] (enregistrer). [[a PREsent]] (un cadeau) / [[to preSENT]] (présenter). [[an OBject]] (un objet) / [[to obJECT]] (s'opposer).

lesson.text: Piège de francophone : en anglais, le **h se prononce presque toujours** ([[house]], [[happy]], [[hockey]]) : ne l'avale pas ! Seuls quelques mots ont un h muet : [[hour]], [[honest]], [[honour]], [[heir]]. C'est pour ça qu'on dit [[an hour]] et [[an honest answer]], mais [[a house]].

Le sais-tu ? Il y a très longtemps, on prononçait vraiment le k de [[knight]] et de [[knife]] ! Le son a disparu, mais l'orthographe est restée. Et [[Wednesday]] vient du vieil anglais : c'était « le jour de Woden », un dieu ancien. Voilà pourquoi il y a un d qu'on n'entend plus.

reading.title: Word Nerds: Episode Twelve
reading.text:
Maya: Welcome back to Word Nerds, the podcast where two students from Ottawa try to figure out why English is so strange. I'm Maya.

Ethan: And I'm Ethan. Today's question comes from a listener in Gatineau named Léa. She writes: “Why is there a b in doubt if nobody pronounces it?”

Maya: Great question, Léa, and the answer is a little surprising. Hundreds of years ago, English borrowed this word from French, and it was spelled without any b at all. Later, some scholars decided that English words should look more like Latin. The Latin word had a b, so they added one. Nobody ever started pronouncing it, though.

Ethan: So the b is basically a decoration?

Maya: Pretty much. The same thing happened with receipt, which got its p from Latin. And island got an s because people thought it was related to the word isle. It isn't, by the way.

Ethan: Okay, but what about knight? Was the k always silent?

Maya: No! Centuries ago, people really pronounced it. Over time, the sound disappeared, but the spelling stayed the same.

Ethan: That's the real problem, isn't it? Pronunciation kept changing, but spelling became fixed once books started being printed.

Maya: Exactly. Printing helped make spelling stable, but people never stopped changing the way they talked. That's why though, through, tough and cough look alike but sound completely different.

Ethan: So, Maya, what's the lesson for our listeners?

Maya: Don't trust your eyes. Listen to real speakers, and when in doubt, check a dictionary. And Léa, you were right to doubt that b!

Ethan: Thanks for listening, everyone. Next week, we'll find out why Wednesday is so hard to spell.

questions.q: Why did scholars add a b to doubt?
choices: To make it easier to pronounce
Because the French word had a b
To make it look more like the Latin word

questions.q: According to Maya, why does island have an s?
choices: People wrongly thought it was related to isle.
The s used to be pronounced.
It comes from the Latin word for water.

questions.q: Why do though, through, tough and cough look alike but sound different?
choices: They come from four different languages.
Scholars invented them as a joke.
Pronunciation kept changing after spelling became fixed.
Printers changed their spelling every year.

questions.q: What does Maya mean by “you were right to doubt that b”?
choices: Léa should start pronouncing the b.
Léa was right to suspect that the b has no role in pronunciation.
Léa made a spelling mistake in her question.
The b will soon be removed from dictionaries.

questions.q: What can we guess about the next episode?
choices: It will be the last episode.
It will be about French words only.
It will explain the strange spelling of a day of the week.

questions.q: What is the main message of the episode?
choices: English spelling often hides history, so don't rely only on how a word looks.
English spelling is random and has no history.
Silent letters should be pronounced carefully.
